tldr: Existing robot world models trained mostly on successful demonstrations fail completely to predict physical behaviors like tilting or slipping when a grasp goes wrong. In this work, the authors built Reforge, a large-scale simulation dataset with intentional failures, and proposed WorldReforge, a framework that self-supervises contact regions and physical surface tracking. Without adding any inference cost, WorldReforge dramatically improves dynamics prediction during contact and failure.
hero_caption: An overview of the WorldReforge training framework. For a Diffusion Transformer (DiT)-based world model, two auxiliary physical losses are introduced: Interaction Alignment (IA), which prioritizes reconstruction on the contact region, and Surface Correspondence (SC), which aligns trajectories of identical object surface points in feature space. Because neither is needed at inference time, physical prediction performance is enhanced with zero additional computational cost.
overview:
Action-conditioned world models that predict future visual frames from robot actions have gained significant attention for autonomous planning and policy evaluation. However, the vast majority of training data for existing models consists of clean demonstrations where humans or robots succeed—the so-called "happy path." As a result, these models suffer from a severe bias: they cannot predict failure physics when a fingertip is misaligned by a few millimeters or a gripper closes slightly too early, causing an object to be pushed, tilted, or slipped. In fact, evaluating major pretrained models revealed that they perform no better than, or even worse than, a static baseline that simply copies the first frame over and over.

To overcome this issue using the strengths of simulation, the authors propose WorldReforge. By introducing slight perturbations to grasp target positions, orientations, and closure timings in simulation, they created Reforge, a dataset of 62k trajectories capturing diverse failure behaviors such as pushing, tilting, and slipping. Furthermore, using accurate 3D object poses and surface geometry from the simulator, they designed two auxiliary losses that train the world model's backbone without adding any inference compute: Interaction Alignment (IA), which emphasizes reconstruction in small contact regions that are typically overshadowed by the rest of the image, and Surface Correspondence (SC), which matches how object surface points move over time at the feature level.

Experiments on Cosmos3 Nano show that WorldReforge reduces object trajectory error by 28.2% overall and by 35.0% on unseen objects. It also lowers the error in predicting how outcomes diverge between two different actions by 43.3%. Remarkably, despite being trained purely in simulation, it also improves reconstruction on real-robot data (DROID) and real failure videos. Controlled data studies further reveal complementary roles between failure and success data: failed contact teaches how objects respond, whereas successful holding teaches how a grasped state persists.
contributions: Quantitatively diagnosed and demonstrated the severity of the "happy-path bias" in existing pretrained world models, which perform on par with or worse than a static baseline that simply copies the first frame during contact failures.

Constructed the Reforge dataset, comprising 62k simulated trajectories pairing perturbed positions, orientations, and timings with dense 3D ground-truth physics, along with 300 real-robot failure trajectories for real-world evaluation.

Proposed WorldReforge, featuring two auxiliary training objectives (IA to emphasize contact-region reconstruction and SC to track object surface points) using simulator geometry with zero added inference cost.

Demonstrated significant improvements in physical prediction and visual quality on unseen objects and real-world videos (e.g., DROID), while uncovering the complementary roles of failed contact and successful holding in learning dynamics.

sections.heading: World models do not know what happens when things go wrong
sections.summary: While action-conditioned world models hold great promise for policy evaluation and planning, existing models are trained primarily on successful demonstrations and fail to predict physical behavior when grasps miss. This section highlights the grim reality that major pretrained models perform no better than a static baseline copying the first frame, and explains the goal of WorldReforge in teaching failure dynamics using dense simulation ground truth.
sections.details:
For robots to act intelligently, they must be able to accurately simulate counterfactual outcomes, such as "what happens if I move right?" or "what happens if I miss the object?" In manipulation, however, meeting this requirement is extremely challenging. When a fingertip is misaligned by a centimeter or a gripper closes a fraction of a second too early, objects do not remain static; they are pushed, tilted, or slip through the fingers. Yet, because existing robot training data is dominated by clean, successful demonstrations, world models have barely learned this "physics of contact."

When the authors evaluated five pretrained world models across three model families, they uncovered a striking result: object-motion prediction error during contact failures was at most 10.4% lower than that of a static baseline that simply copies the first image, and two models were actually worse than this baseline. Even as an object was pushed or tipped over, the models predicted it staying frozen in its initial pose. Under such predictions, policies executing erroneous actions would be falsely evaluated as having made no mistake.

Collecting failure data on physical robots poses serious safety and cost challenges. Simulation, however, allows safe, abundant, and millimeter-level controlled generation of failures. Crucially, simulators provide ground truth for accurate 3D poses, contact states, and surface geometry. WorldReforge leverages this simulator ground truth to instill failure physics into world models without adding a single flop at inference time.

sections.heading: The evolution of world models and the challenge of physical alignment
sections.summary: This section reviews prior work in action-conditioned video prediction, latent dynamics models, and fine-tuning with failure data. It identifies key limitations of existing approaches: relying on global image reconstruction losses or coarse success/failure signals leaves them unable to capture fine-grained object motion in small contact regions.
sections.details:
This section organizes related work into three main categories:

### 2.1 The lineage of robot world models
World models have evolved rapidly, from early pixel prediction to latent-space dynamics models like PlaNet and DreamerV3, language-conditioned variants, and recent large-scale video and action foundation models like UniSim, Cosmos3, DreamDojo, and LingBot-VA. Nevertheless, these models still struggle with contact-driven object predictions, especially when representing failure dynamics.

### 2.2 Post-training for physical alignment
To learn from failures, methods such as FACT, CureWM, counterfactual modeling, or reward-guided approaches like DreamTrue and HF-WM have been proposed. However, existing methods suffer from two fundamental limitations. First, contact dynamics occur in tiny fractions of the image frame, meaning global image reconstruction losses underweight and ignore them. Second, scalar signals like success or reward cannot guide the detailed physical trajectories of how objects move. WorldReforge overcomes both barriers using dense geometric ground truth from simulation.

### 2.3 Video and interaction evaluation
Conventional video generation metrics (PSNR, SSIM, VBench) focus on visual appeal and are insufficient for measuring action-dependent physical correctness. This work adopts point tracking (e.g., CoTracker) to separately measure object and gripper motion errors (ADE/FDE), and introduces an evaluation protocol measuring how predictions diverge under two distinct actions.

sections.heading: WorldReforge: Drilling physics into models via simulation ground truth
sections.summary: This section describes how the 62k-trajectory Reforge dataset was built and details the two core auxiliary losses in WorldReforge: IA and SC. Interaction Alignment focuses reconstruction on contact regions, while Surface Correspondence forces backbone features to directly track object surface points over time, achieving physical fidelity without extra inference parameters.
sections.details:
The proposed approach targets action-conditioned video prediction models based on diffusion or Flow Matching. Given an initial frame $I_0$ and a sequence of robot actions, the task is to generate future frames.

### 3.2 Constructing the Reforge dataset
Using a robot simulator, the authors first generate nominal successful grasps via tools like cuRobo. They then introduce intentional perturbations to end-effector translation, rotation, and gripper closure timing. This produces 62,425 trajectories across 96 object assets covering a wide range of outcomes, including misses, pushes, tilts, and slips. Among these, 13,577 trajectories involve contact failures. For evaluation, they also collected Reforge-Real, consisting of 300 real failure trajectories using a physical Franka Panda arm.

### 3.3.1 Interaction Alignment (IA): Concentrated learning on contact regions
Under standard global reconstruction losses, errors in small objects or fingertip contacts are drowned out by vast background pixels. IA addresses this by projecting the object's 3D bounding box to form a soft mask $M$. The difference between the predicted clean latent $\hat{z}_0$ and the ground-truth latent $z_0$ is computed only within this masked region and normalized by the mask's total area. This ensures that even when an object occupies a small corner of the screen, sufficient gradient signal reaches the backbone.

### 3.3.2 Surface Correspondence (SC): Tracking surface points over time
While IA corrects spatial appearance and localization, SC enforces temporal physical continuity. Specifying a 3D point on the object's surface in the simulator allows its exact future 2D projection (pixel coordinates) to be computed using camera intrinsics/extrinsics and object transformation matrices. SC extracts intermediate features from the DiT backbone, computes cosine similarities between the initial surface point feature and candidate spatial features in future frames, and applies a softmax to obtain a predicted location $\hat{p}_{it}$. The Euclidean distance between this predicted position and the projected ground-truth position forms the loss to supervise the backbone directly.

Crucially, both IA and SC serve strictly as training-time loss functions. They introduce no new layers or extra inference steps. The existing architecture of the world model remains untouched, while its grasp of physics is dramatically reinforced.

captions.F2: Hierarchical taxonomy of the Reforge dataset. The top row illustrates the perturbation types applied at execution time (translation, rotation, and grasp timing) and trajectory counts, while the bottom row shows the resulting physical outcomes, such as contact occurrence, object pushing or tilting, and final grasp stability. Rather than an unannotated video collection, it features dense physical ground truth.
captions.F3: Architecture and training pipeline of WorldReforge. Alongside the standard Flow Matching loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}$), the model is post-trained using two auxiliary objectives: a region-weighted reconstruction loss using geometric masks (IA) and a surface-point tracking loss using backbone features (SC).

sections.heading: Unseen objects and real-world videos: Dramatic gains in physical accuracy
sections.summary: Validation was performed across five models from three families: Cosmos3, DreamDojo, and LingBot-VA. Applying WorldReforge substantially reduced object motion errors and showed strong generalization to assets never seen during training. Furthermore, despite being trained solely in simulation, it improved reconstruction quality on real failure videos and the DROID dataset.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental setup
Training used 25.6k interaction segments from the Reforge dataset (roughly half of which were failure trajectories), post-training on eight NVIDIA H200 GPUs. Evaluations were conducted on a simulation evaluation set (Reforge-Eval), a large-scale real-robot dataset (DROID), and a real failure set (Reforge-Real). Metrics included object and gripper average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) computed via CoTracker, video reconstruction quality (PSNR, SSIM), and visual quality pass rates (Q) judged by an MLLM (Qwen3.8-27B).

### 4.2 Quantitative results
The authors compared the base pretrained models (Pretrained), models trained on Reforge with standard losses (Reforge), and the proposed method with IA and SC (WorldReforge).
- **Physical response accuracy**: On Cosmos3 Nano, WorldReforge reduced object ADE by 28.2% compared to Pretrained. Compared to Reforge trained under the same data and compute budget, ADE was further reduced by 4.4% and final-frame position error (FDE) by 5.0%.
- **Consistency across model families**: Significant improvements were observed on DreamDojo and LingBot-VA as well, proving that WorldReforge's loss formulation is broadly applicable across architectures.
- **Generalization to unseen objects**: For unseen object assets not encountered during training, Cosmos3 Nano achieved a 35.02% reduction in object ADE over the pretrained model and a 4.44 dB boost in PSNR. This confirms the model learned general contact dynamics rather than memorizing specific object shapes.
- **Sim-to-Real transfer**: Despite being post-trained strictly on simulation data, PSNR improved by 1.04 dB on real-robot DROID videos and by 0.68 dB on Reforge-Real. Predictions did not collapse on real-world failures, achieving a 100% visual quality pass rate.

sections.heading: Why it works: Dissecting failure data and physical guidance
sections.summary: This section provides an in-depth analysis of action-dependent branching, execution variations, and the respective roles of successful holding versus failed contact. In particular, the error in predicting how outcomes diverge between two actions dropped by 43.3%, revealing that failed contact teaches object response while successful holding teaches state persistence.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Execution variations and coverage
The authors investigated the impact of translation, rotation, and grasp-timing variations during training. Combining translation and rotation perturbations yielded the best object-motion accuracy (ADE 7.25 px). However, accurately predicting the gripper's own trajectory required including variations in grasp closure timing. A balanced mixture of both is essential.

### 5.2 The complementary roles of success and failure
Examining models trained on "failure data only" versus "success data only" revealed an intriguing dynamic. Adding "failed contact" data—where the gripper closes but fails to secure the object—drastically improved object ADE during failed contacts by 18.0% (from 12.78 px to 10.48 px). However, when predicting "holding" (lifting and maintaining a grasped object), the model trained solely on successful data performed best. In short, failed contact teaches how touched objects move (change), while successful grasps teach how a grasped state remains stable (persistence).

### 5.3 Action-dependent responses
A world model's utility for planning hinges on whether its predicted futures correctly diverge when taking Action A versus Action B. On 100 paired trajectories sharing the same initial frame but different actions, the authors measured Response Difference Error (RDE)—the squared error between predicted and true visual divergence. WorldReforge reduced RDE by 43.3% compared to the pretrained model. As shown in Figure F4, in branches where one action slips and the other lifts successfully, contact-area residuals are dramatically smaller.

### 5.4 Ablation of physical auxiliary losses
Evaluating IA (region reconstruction) and SC (surface tracking) individually versus jointly showed that combining them lowered object ADE by an additional 3.2% and gripper ADE by 6.3%. Furthermore, comparing SC trained with true simulator ground truth against SC trained with CoTracker pseudo-labels showed that true physical geometry kept object ADE roughly 4% lower, validating the advantage of direct 3D geometric supervision.

captions.F4: Comparison of response divergence from the same initial frame under two different actions (Action A: grasp slips; Action B: successful lift). The bottom row displays RMS residual error maps across future frames, where darker indicates closer alignment with ground truth. WorldReforge (right) exhibits noticeably lower errors (RDE) around the object and contact areas compared to Pretrained (left) and Reforge alone (center), capturing action-dependent branching with high fidelity.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future outlook
sections.summary: WorldReforge significantly improves contact prediction in action-conditioned world models by combining simulated failure experiences with geometric physical supervision. Demonstrating that both successes and failures are essential, future work aims to scale to longer horizons and integrate into closed-loop control.
sections.details: This work challenges the convention of training robot world models almost exclusively on happy-path demonstrations. Through the Reforge dataset of diverse simulated failures and the WorldReforge framework combining contact-focused IA and surface-tracking SC, the authors substantially advance contact-driven object dynamics modeling without incurring extra inference overhead.\n\nA key insight is the complementary nature of training data: failed contacts teach dynamic object responses, while successful grasps teach state persistence. Promising directions for future work include extending predictions over longer time horizons for complex multi-stage manipulation and integrating accurate early failure predictions into closed-loop control to trigger real-time trajectory corrections.

sections.heading: Appendix: Real-robot setup and qualitative results
sections.summary: This section summarizes the hardware configuration for the Reforge-Real dataset and qualitative prediction comparisons across various objects. The results confirm accurate reproduction of pushing and tilting dynamics in both simulation and real-world settings.
sections.details:
### A.5 Reforge-Real collection environment
The real-world evaluation dataset, Reforge-Real, was collected using a 7-DoF Franka Panda robot arm and its stock electric gripper. Three synchronized cameras recorded at 640×544 resolution: a wrist-mounted Stereolabs ZED-M camera (gripper view) and two externally fixed Intel RealSense cameras (left and right shoulder views). Operators deliberately executed failing grasp maneuvers via teleoperation on 10 everyday tabletop objects (plush toys, fruit, spray cans, etc.), recording 300 failure sequences.

### E Qualitative prediction comparisons
Predictions were compared against baselines across known simulation assets (sauce bottles, markers), unseen assets (Rubik's cube, red mug), and real-world videos from DROID and Reforge-Real. In pretrained world models, objects frequently stayed frozen in place even as the robot gripper collided with them. In contrast, WorldReforge sharply reproduced the object rotating, getting pushed backward, or slipping out upon contact across all three viewpoints with high geometric consistency.

captions.F5: Data collection setup for the real-robot failure dataset, Reforge-Real. Synchronized three-view footage from a wrist camera (ZED-M) on a 7-DoF Franka Panda arm and two external cameras (RealSense) captures diverse failed grasp interactions on everyday objects.
captions.F7: Three-view prediction comparisons in simulation. The top two rows feature training objects, while the bottom two feature unseen objects. Whereas the Pretrained model (middle) keeps objects virtually frozen in place, WorldReforge (bottom) accurately reproduces contact-induced tilting, rotation, and displacement matching ground truth (top).
captions.F8: Prediction comparisons on real-world videos (DROID and Reforge-Real). WorldReforge, trained purely on simulation, accurately tracks contact dynamics such as pushing a strawberry or toppling a plastic bottle in real environments without visual degradation.

takeaways: World models trained only on successful demonstrations collapse into static predictions copying the first frame during contact failures, risking dangerous overestimation during policy evaluation and simulation.
The true value of simulation lies in safely and infinitely generating slight execution perturbations paired with complete 3D geometric ground truth.

Standard global reconstruction losses fail to capture localized contact dynamics; area-normalized contact reconstruction (IA) and feature-space surface point tracking (SC) are highly effective remedies.
Failure data is not a silver bullet on its own: failed contact teaches object response while successful grasping teaches state persistence, making a balanced mixture of both essential.
limitations: The evaluated prediction horizon is relatively short (16 frames, or a few seconds), leaving physical consistency over long-horizon, multi-stage manipulation tasks unverified.
While visual reconstruction improvements (PSNR, etc.) were demonstrated during Sim-to-Real transfer, fine-grained 3D object motion errors were not quantitatively measured on physical hardware.
Because training relies on accurate 3D bounding boxes and mesh surface points provided by the simulator, the post-training pipeline cannot be applied directly to unannotated real-world data alone.
